title: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
shortTitle: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH

s1_definition.oneliner: PUT replaces the whole resource so missing fields get cleared, while PATCH changes only the fields you send and everything else stays untouched.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **PUT** – performs a full replacement of a resource; the body is the entire new representation, so any omitted field is set to default or cleared.
- **PATCH** – performs a partial update; the client sends only the changed fields, and the server leaves every other field untouched.
- **Idempotency** – PUT is idempotent by definition because sending the same full body twice produces the same state; PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent.
- **Validation** – PUT validates the full object because every field must be present; PATCH validates only the fields that are present.
- **Null handling** – a simple merge-patch cannot distinguish between "field is null" (delete it) and "field is absent" (do not touch it), which is why JSON Merge Patch and JSON Patch formats exist.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Priya's profile form at National Bank of India. PUT is like handing the clerk a brand new, fully filled form that completely replaces the old one: if you left the phone number blank, the clerk erases the old phone number too, because the new form is now the truth. PATCH is like handing the clerk a sticky note that says "only change the phone number to this": everything else on the existing form stays exactly as it was.

sections.s6_takeaway:
PUT and PATCH both update a resource but they mean very different things. PUT is a full replacement: the client sends the complete representation, and the server replaces the entire resource, so any field the client leaves out is cleared or set to default. PATCH is a partial update: the client sends only the fields it wants to change, and the server leaves every other field exactly as it was.

A direct consequence is idempotency. PUT is idempotent because sending the same full body twice ends in the same state both times, which makes it safe to retry after a timeout. PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent, because a PATCH that expresses a relative change like "add one hundred to the balance" would stack up if repeated.

At National Bank of India this distinction prevented a real bug. Priya wanted to change only the nickname of her saved landlord beneficiary. When the app sent only the nickname through an endpoint that behaved like PUT, the account number and IFSC were wiped out because PUT treats missing fields as cleared, and her next rent payment failed. The fix was to use PATCH for partial edits so only the nickname changed and the other fields survived, and to reserve PUT for cases where the customer genuinely re-submits a complete form such as full KYC.

The careful detail is validation and null handling. For PUT, validate the full object because every field must be present. For PATCH, validate only the fields that are present. And because a simple ignore-nulls merge cannot tell the difference between "change this to null" and "do not touch this," adopt JSON Merge Patch where null means delete, or JSON Patch for fully explicit operations. Choosing the right verb and being precise about missing fields is what keeps partial updates safe.

Remember one sentence: PUT replaces the whole resource and clears missing fields, while PATCH changes only the fields you send and leaves everything else untouched.

---

keyPoints: PUT performs a full replacement where missing fields are cleared or set to default.
PATCH performs a partial update where only the sent fields are changed and everything else is preserved.
PUT is idempotent by definition; PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent because relative changes can stack.
PUT validates the full object; PATCH validates only the fields that are present.
Null handling in PATCH requires care: JSON Merge Patch uses null to delete, JSON Patch uses an explicit remove operation.
Use PUT for complete re-submissions like KYC, and PATCH for day-to-day edits like changing a nickname.
